name: Ligurian (Genoese)
variety: Genoese, the urban variety of Genoa that serves as the Ligurian koine, in the official spelling of the Académia Ligùstica do Brénno
sources: Toso, Fiorenzo (1997). Grammatica del genovese: varietà urbana e di koinè. Recco: Le Mani.
Forner, Werner (1988). Italienisch: Areallinguistik I. Ligurien. In Holtus, Metzeltin and Schmitt (eds.), Lexikon der Romanistischen Linguistik, volume IV. Tübingen: Niemeyer.
Forner, Werner (1997). Liguria. In Maiden and Parry (eds.), The Dialects of Italy. London: Routledge.
Ghini, Mirco (2001). Asymmetries in the Phonology of Miogliola. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
contrasts: vowel length in stressed syllables for every vowel quality, shown in the official spelling (long vowels with a circumflex, ö for long [ɔː] and æ for long [ɛː]; short stressed vowels with an acute or grave): amîgo [aˈmiːɡu], mâ [maː], against tùtto [ˈtytu], neutte [ˈnøte]
front rounded vowels /y ø/ next to /i e/ and /u/ (written u, eu; written o is [u])
open-mid versus close-mid front vowels /ɛ e/

velar nasal /ŋ/ versus alveolar /n/ between vowels: the velar nasal continues Latin single n and is written nn- or ñ (lùnn-a [ˈlyŋa] 'moon', campann-a 'bell'), while Latin double nn gives [n] (pénna [ˈpena] 'feather')
voiced versus voiceless sibilants /s z/ and /ʃ ʒ/ (written s, ç, z, sc, x)
affricates /tʃ dʒ/; there are no /ts dz/ and no /ʎ/ (figgio, famiggia have /dʒ/)
allophony: /n/ is velar [ŋ] at the end of a word and before any consonant (pan [paŋ], canto [ˈkaŋtu])
a consonant after a short stressed vowel is somewhat lengthened and is written double (neutte, tutto, dònna); after a long vowel it is short. Consonant length is not distinctive by itself
stressed vowels are long before r plus consonant (càrta) and in many open penultimate syllables
/r/ is a weak alveolar tap; between vowels and at the end of infinitives it was lost in the urban dialect (scignoa 'lady', mangiâ 'to eat')
vowels before the velar nasal are nasalised to some degree
unstressed vowels keep their quality; long vowels also occur in unstressed syllables before the stress, written with a diaeresis
/s/ before a voiced consonant is [z]; written s between vowels is [z], ss and ç are [s]
phonotactics: words end in a vowel or in the velar nasal; other final consonants occur in loanwords
sequences of vowels are frequent because of lost consonants (moæ, poæ, scignoa)

stress.rule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of most words and on the last syllable of words that end in a long vowel (infinitives such as mangiâ, finî; çittæ) or in a stressed vowel plus nasal; the official spelling marks stress and length with accents.
stress.cues: duration (with the vowel length contrast realised in the stressed syllable), pitch and intensity

rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements for Ligurian are known to us. Length of the stressed vowel and of the following consonant are in inverse relation.

length.notes: Vowel length is distinctive under stress. Double consonants of the spelling mark a preceding short vowel and are only slightly longer than single ones, unlike Italian geminates. No duration ratios are cited here.

intonation.declarative: fall on or after the last stressed syllable to a low ending
intonation.yes_no_question: no change of word order; rise at the end of the utterance
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then a fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: rise through the stressed syllable, helped by the long vowels
intonation.notes: Genoese speech is popularly said to have a marked sing-song melody, but the intonation of Ligurian has not been described in the sources used here. The entries are general northern Italian patterns and should be read as low confidence.

problems: the velar nasal between vowels is lost: nn- is read as plain [n] (lùnn-a [lˈyna], penn-a [pˈena], bonn-a [bˈuna]), so penn-a and pénna sound the same
the hyphen of nn-a also upsets the stress: campann-a is stressed on the first syllable ([kˈaŋpana])
the long vowel written êu is not recognised: fêugo is [fˈeːyːɡu] instead of [ˈføːɡu]
lengoa is [leŋɡˈua] with stress on u; the expected form is [ˈleŋɡwa]
double consonants get a half-length mark in the IPA output only; their duration in the synthesis is that of single consonants
/r/ is the base trill, where Genoese has a weak tap
intonation uses one of the generic tune sets (voice option 'intonation 2')
good: sixteen vowel phonemes: eight qualities including [y] and [ø], each short and long (about 150 to 180 against 230 to 260 table units)
the letter values of the official spelling: o as [u], u as [y], eu as [ø], æ as [ɛː], x as [ʒ], ç as [s], z as [z]
final and pre-consonantal n is velar [ŋ] (pan [pˈaŋ], gianco [dʒˈaŋku])
stressed vowels are lengthened before r plus consonant (càrta [kˈaːrta])

notes: Ligurian varieties differ a good deal (western, central, eastern, Oltregiogo, and the colonial varieties of Monaco, Bonifacio and Carloforte); this profile is for Genoese only. Several spellings are in use; the rules expect the official one with accents for length and stress.
